items.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: So I just started thinking of topics off the top of my head, like Chicago jazz, and he went right to the Beiderbecke-Trumbauer, and this and that, and John Kirby, which is a little offshoot and some of that stuff thrown in.

ctx.x: It really was, yeah. It took a fairly long period of six months to a year of really thinking back and asking myself well how did I learn to do this, and what records or what players did I listen to to develop this kind of technique or this way of playing and this approach to harmony, where did I learn this way of the rhythm section working together that was a little more conversational and not so style specific. So it was a really great learning experience for me. One of the people that was really helpful in…

history. It’s called Jazz Styles, it’s Mark Gridley. And when I knew I was going to have to put a jazz history course together there were so many deficiencies in my background of things that I didn’t know about, so I called Harvey, and he graciously gave up a lot of his time. I think I went over there for three or four Saturdays for four or five hours. And he had a huge record collection. There was a room in his apartment about a fourth of the size of this room that was just floor to ceiling shelves. And he knew…

Do you think there’s a difference in what you did back then as — I mean you were a student of the music, even while you were teaching. And you had to go to these lengths of what you just described. Nowadays everything’s under your fingers and is available at a moment’s notice, and I’ve been trying to figure out whether this is good or bad or both.
